steps.body: Measuring the same object in a different unit changes the NUMBER but never the amount. A rope is 3 meters and also 300 centimeters: 100 centimeters make a meter, the same equal-lengths rule the length ladder shows for millimeters, centimeters, meters, and kilometers.
steps.narration: Measuring the same object in a different unit changes the NUMBER but never the amount. A rope is 3 meters and also 300 centimeters: 100 centimeters make a meter, the same equal-lengths rule the length ladder shows for millimeters, centimeters, meters, and kilometers.

widget.prompt: How many centimeters in 3 meters? Hop one meter at a time.

commonLandings.feedback: Two meter-hops reach 200 cm; the rope is three meters long.
Four hops overshoot — three meters is 300 centimeters.

widget.missFeedback: Each meter is 100 centimeters, so three of them reach 300.
widget.successFeedback: 300 — three meter-hops, each worth 100 centimeters. Same rope, bigger number.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — each meter is 100 centimeters, so three of them reach 300.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — three meters stops exactly at 300 centimeters.

predict.prompt: A rope is 3 m. In centimeters, is the number bigger or smaller?
predict.reveal: Centimeters are smaller, so many more of them fit along the same rope — 300 instead of 3; run it the other way and the bigger unit means fewer of them cover the same rope, so the number shrinks.

cml.actionGoal: Keep one length fixed while changing its unit and compare the resulting counts.
invariants: Equivalent measurements describe the same length; the smaller unit produces the larger count.
misconceptions: Treating a larger unit as if it must create a larger numerical measure.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the unit got ten times smaller, what would happen to the number that measures the same object?

widget.prompt: The same rope is measured in meters and in centimeters. Which measurement has the LARGER number?

options.label: Centimeters use smaller units
options.feedback: Correct — smaller units means more of them fit, so the count rises even though the rope never changes.

options.label: Meters, because meters are bigger
options.feedback: Bigger units give a SMALLER count: fewer of them cover the same rope.

options.label: They are the same number
options.feedback: The length is the same, but the NUMBER differs because the units differ — 3 m and 300 cm.

options.label: It depends on the rope
options.feedback: It does not: for any length, the smaller unit always yields the larger count.

steps.narration: Smaller units need more of them to cover the same length, so the number always moves opposite to the unit size.

widget.prompt: Compare a second fixed length: how many centimeters are in 2 meters? Hop one meter at a time.

commonLandings.feedback: One hop is only one meter, or 100 centimeters; the rope is two meters.
Three hops overshoot; two meters is 200 centimeters.

widget.missFeedback: Each meter is 100 centimeters, so two equal hops reach 200.
widget.successFeedback: 200 centimeters — two meter-hops of 100 centimeters each.
widget.lowFeedback: This landing is short of two complete meter-hops.
widget.highFeedback: This landing is past two complete meter-hops.

widget.prompt: Apply without the opening model: A route measures 2 kilometers, and each kilometer is 1000 meters. Compute 2 × 1000.

commonErrors.feedback: Adding mixes a quantity with a rate. Each of the 2 kilometers contributes 1000 meters, so they multiply.
That divided. Going to the SMALLER unit needs more of them, so the number must grow.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Name the quantity and the conversion factor, then decide whether the count should grow or shrink.

widget.prompt: Diagnose a new comparison: why is the number 2,000 in 2,000 meters larger than the number 2 in 2 kilometers?

options.label: Meters are smaller units, so more are needed
options.feedback: Correct — both measurements name the same distance, but meters use the smaller unit.

options.label: Kilometers measure a different distance
options.feedback: The distance is unchanged: 2 kilometers and 2,000 meters are equivalent.

options.label: The larger number means the distance grew
options.feedback: Only the unit and numerical count changed; the distance did not.

options.label: The comparison depends on the route
options.feedback: For any fixed distance, changing from kilometers to meters multiplies the count by 1,000.

widget.prompt: A ribbon measures 4 meters, which is 400 centimeters. Which operation correctly turns 4 into 400?

options.label: Multiply 4 by 100
options.feedback: Correct — each meter equals 100 centimeters, so multiplying 4 by 100 gives 400 centimeters.

options.label: Add 100 to 4
options.feedback: Adding 100 only once mixes a rate with a count; every one of the 4 meters needs its own factor of 100.

options.label: Divide 4 by 100
options.feedback: Dividing shrinks the number, but centimeters are the smaller unit, so the count must grow instead.

options.label: Multiply 4 by 10
options.feedback: Ten converts centimeters to millimeters; meters to centimeters uses the factor 100, not 10.
